title: Even Baron’s line admits grace-persuasion follows justification — it is not the justifying act
source_text: CII. Sed praeterea hic est quaestio specialis de actu per quem fides justificat, & ratione cujus justificatio fidei tribuitur. Nam illi ipsi qui docent firmam persuasionem, qua statuimus Christum nos pretioso suo sanguine redemisse, & Deum Patrem propter ejus meritum omnia nostra peccata remisisse, esse praecipuum & specificum actum fidei justificantis, illi, inquam, quod mirum videri possit, agnoscunt nihilominus hanc persuasionem non esse actum quo fides justificat, sed qui justificationem jam factam consequitur: ut supra ostendimus de Roberto Baronio, Riveto, Wendelino, Amesio, & Paraeo. Qui omnes fidem describentes per fiduciam illam qua de Dei gratia erga nos certi sumus, & persuasum habemus peccata nostra esse per Christum condonata, simul tamen docent hanc persuasionem non esse actum per quem justificamur.
pass_a_gloss: But besides there is here a special question concerning the act through which faith justifies, and by reason of which justification is attributed to faith. For those very ones who teach that the firm persuasion by which we lay down that Christ has redeemed us by his precious blood, and that God the Father for his merit has remitted all our sins, is the chief and specific act of justifying faith — they, I say, what may seem strange, nevertheless acknowledge that this persuasion is not the act by which faith justifies, but that which follows justification already made: as we showed above concerning Robert Baron, Rivetus, Wendelin, Ames, and Paraeus. Who all, describing faith by that trust by which we are certain of God's grace toward us, and have it persuaded that our sins have been forgiven through Christ, yet at the same time teach that this persuasion is not the act through which we are justified.
pass_b_english: Separate question: which act is the one through which faith justifies?
Oddly, even those who call past-tense redemption/remission persuasion faith’s chief specific act (Baron, Rivetus, Wendelin, Ames, Paraeus) still admit it is not the act by which faith justifies.
It follows justification already done — they teach both at once.

lemmas.latin: non esse actum quo fides justificat, sed qui justificationem jam factam consequitur
lemmas.gloss: is not the act by which faith justifies, but that which follows justification already made

choices.why: Le Blanc flags the inconsistency in Baron’s line.
rejected: They hold persuasion both defines and formally justifies
